title: Les pronoms sujets
summary: The six words that tell you who is doing the action — and the two traps English speakers fall into.

blocks.text: Every French verb needs a subject. Unlike Spanish or Italian, you cannot drop it. There are six persons, but French splits 'you' into two and has a pronoun, on, that English has no equivalent for.

head: French
English
Notes
rows: becomes j' before a vowel or silent h: j'ai, j'habite
friends, family, children, colleagues you know well
on takes the same verb form as il
a stranger, a boss — or any group of people
elles only if every person is female

blocks.text: On is the single most useful pronoun in spoken French. It means 'we' in casual speech (On va au cinéma) and 'one/people in general' in writing (En France, on dîne tard). It always takes the il form of the verb, even when it means 'we': on va, never 'on allons'.

items.fr: Je m'appelle Tien et j'habite au Canada.
items.en: My name is Tien and I live in Canada.
items.note: je → j' twice, before m'appelle? No — before habite only. Je m'appelle keeps je because m is a consonant.

items.fr: Vous êtes prêts ? On y va !
items.en: Are you ready? Let's go!
items.note: on = we, with the il form of aller

items.fr: Mes sœurs sont médecins ; elles travaillent à Lyon.
items.en: My sisters are doctors; they work in Lyon.
items.note: all female → elles

blocks.text: A group of ninety-nine women and one man is ils. French grammar is not fair, but it is consistent.
Choosing tu or vous is a social decision, not a grammar one. Start with vous with anyone you have just met; they will invite you to switch with on peut se tutoyer.

practice.q: Which pronoun do you use for your new manager?
practice.why: vous is the formal singular — a manager you have just met.
je becomes j' before the vowel of habite.

practice.q: Which verb form goes with on?
practice.why: on always takes the third person singular, even when it means 'we'.

practice.q: Marie et Sophie sont là. ___ sont en retard.
practice.why: Two women, so the feminine plural elles.

title: Le verbe être
summary: Irregular, unavoidable, and the auxiliary behind half the past tense.

blocks.text: Être links a subject to a description: a job, a nationality, an adjective, a place. When it links to a job or a nationality, French drops the article that English keeps: Je suis médecin, not 'je suis un médecin'.

items.fr: Je suis vietnamien et je vis au Canada.
items.en: I'm Vietnamese and I live in Canada.
items.note: no article before a nationality

items.fr: Nous sommes en réunion jusqu'à midi.
items.en: We're in a meeting until noon.

items.fr: C'est mon frère. Il est ingénieur.
items.en: This is my brother. He's an engineer.

blocks.text: English uses 'to be' for age, hunger, thirst and fear. French uses avoir: j'ai 30 ans, j'ai faim, j'ai peur. Saying 'je suis 30 ans' is the single most recognisable beginner mistake.

practice.why: vous → êtes, with a circumflex.

practice.q: How do you say 'I am thirty years old'?
practice.why: Age uses avoir plus the word ans.
il/elle/on → est, and no un before the job.
French omits the article before an unmodified profession.

title: Le verbe avoir
summary: Possession, age, and the auxiliary for most past-tense verbs.

blocks.text: Avoir carries a family of fixed expressions where English reaches for 'to be'. Learn them as whole blocks rather than translating word by word.
Notice the pronunciation trap: ils ont (they have) and ils sont (they are) differ by one sound. The liaison in ils ont makes a z sound; ils sont has a clear s.

practice.why: nous → avons.
Personal sensations of hot and cold use avoir. Il fait froid describes the weather, not you.
ils → ont.
avoir mal à + les dents contracts to aux dents.

title: Les articles définis
summary: French uses 'the' far more often than English does — including in front of whole categories.

head: Form
Used before
Example
rows: any singular starting with a vowel or silent h

blocks.text: Use the definite article for something specific (le livre sur la table), and also — unlike English — for general statements about a whole category and for likes and dislikes.

items.fr: J'aime le café mais je déteste le thé.
items.en: I like coffee but I hate tea.
items.note: general category → definite article, where English uses none

items.fr: Les Canadiens parlent anglais et français.
items.en: Canadians speak English and French.
items.note: a whole nation → les

items.fr: Le français est difficile au début.
items.en: French is difficult at the start.
items.note: languages take le

blocks.text: After the verb parler, the article disappears: je parle français, not 'je parle le français'. But with any other verb it comes back: j'apprends le français, j'aime le français.

practice.why: école begins with a vowel, so le/la both reduce to l'.
A general liking takes the definite article.
Plural, so les regardless of gender.
parler + language drops the article.

title: Les articles indéfinis
summary: A, an, and the plural English does not have a word for.

blocks.text: Des has no English equivalent — English simply uses the bare plural. 'I have friends' is J'ai des amis, never 'j'ai amis'. French will not tolerate a noun with no determiner in front of it.
In a negative sentence, un, une and des all collapse into de (or d'). This rule catches almost every learner.

items.fr: J'ai une voiture. → Je n'ai pas de voiture.
items.en: I have a car. → I don't have a car.

items.fr: Il y a des places libres. → Il n'y a pas de places libres.
items.en: There are free seats. → There are no free seats.

items.fr: C'est un bon restaurant. → Ce n'est pas un bon restaurant.
items.en: It's a good restaurant. → It isn't a good restaurant.
items.note: Exception: after être the article does not change.

blocks.text: The un → de rule applies after a negated verb of having or existing, but never after être. Ce n'est pas un problème keeps un.

practice.q: Je voudrais ___ café, s'il vous plaît.
practice.why: café is masculine singular.
des becomes de after a negation.
A plural noun needs des; French never leaves a noun bare.

practice.q: Which keeps its article after a negation?
practice.why: After être the article survives: ce n'est pas un chien.

title: Les articles partitifs
titleEn: Partitive articles: du, de la, des
summary: How French says 'some' — and why it cannot be left out.

blocks.text: When you are talking about an unmeasured quantity of something — some bread, some water, some patience — French uses the partitive article. English drops it; French cannot.
The choice between le pain and du pain is the choice between the whole idea and part of it. J'aime le pain = I like bread (in general). Je mange du pain = I'm eating some bread (a portion of it).

items.fr: Le matin, je bois du café et je mange du pain.
items.en: In the morning I drink coffee and eat bread.

items.fr: Il faut de la patience pour apprendre une langue.
items.en: You need patience to learn a language.
items.note: abstract nouns take the partitive too

items.fr: Je ne mange pas de viande.
items.en: I don't eat meat.
items.note: after a negation, du/de la/des → de

blocks.text: After any expression of quantity the article vanishes and only de remains: beaucoup de travail, never 'beaucoup du travail'.

practice.q: Je voudrais ___ eau, s'il vous plaît.
practice.why: eau is feminine and starts with a vowel.

practice.q: Il y a beaucoup ___ monde ce soir.
practice.why: After beaucoup, only de.

options: Je ne bois pas du vin.
Je ne bois pas de vin.
Je ne bois pas le vin.
practice.why: The partitive reduces to de in the negative.

practice.q: Which means 'I like cheese in general'?
practice.why: General preference → definite article.

title: Le genre des noms
summary: Every French noun is masculine or feminine. Endings give you good odds, not certainty.

blocks.text: Gender is not about meaning — la table is not feminine for any reason you can reason out. Learn every noun together with its article: not 'table' but la table. The good news is that word endings predict gender correctly about eighty per cent of the time.

Some categories are reliably masculine: days, months, seasons, languages, metals, trees, and most countries not ending in -e. Countries ending in -e are usually feminine: la France, la Chine — but le Mexique is a stubborn exception.
A handful of nouns change meaning with gender. le livre = book, la livre = pound. le tour = a turn or tour, la tour = a tower. le poste = a job, la poste = the post office.
-age words are masculine, but four common ones are not: la page, la plage, l'image, la cage.

practice.why: -tion nouns are feminine.
-ment nouns are masculine.
Feminine la tour is a tower; masculine le tour is a turn or a tour.
-té nouns are feminine.

title: Le pluriel des noms
summary: Add -s, hear nothing, and watch for the six families that break the rule.

blocks.text: The regular plural adds -s, which is silent. In speech the plural is signalled by the article — le livre versus les livres — not by the noun itself. This is why listening for les, des and ces matters so much.

head: Singular ends in
Plural
Example
rows: le fils → les fils, le prix → les prix
le bureau → les bureaux, le jeu → les jeux
le journal → les journaux, l'animal → les animaux
le trou → les trous, but le bijou → les bijoux

items.fr: Les journaux publient les mêmes nouvelles.
items.en: The newspapers publish the same news.

items.fr: Les animaux sauvages vivent dans la forêt.
items.en: Wild animals live in the forest.

items.fr: Monsieur → Messieurs, Madame → Mesdames.
items.en: Sir → Gentlemen, Madam → Ladies.
items.note: both halves of the word change

blocks.text: l'œil becomes les yeux — completely irregular, and unavoidable when talking about eyes.

practice.why: -al becomes -aux.
-eau takes -x, not -s.
Words ending in -x do not change.
Fully irregular.

title: Les verbes en -er au présent
summary: Ninety per cent of French verbs live here. Learn one pattern, unlock a thousand words.

blocks.text: Drop the -er from the infinitive and add the endings below. Four of the six endings are silent, so parle, parles, parle and parlent all sound identical — the subject pronoun does the work of telling them apart.
A few -er verbs adjust their spelling to protect their pronunciation. These are not irregular verbs — they follow the same endings, they just repair the stem.
The stem changes always appear in the four 'boot' forms — je, tu, il, ils — and never in nous and vous. Draw a boot around the conjugation table and you can see it.

practice.why: -ger verbs keep the e before -ons.
ils → -ent, silent.
c → ç before -ons to keep the soft sound.

practice.q: Which two forms sound different from the rest?
practice.why: Only -ons and -ez are pronounced; the other four endings are silent.

title: Les verbes en -ir au présent
summary: The -iss- group: finir, choisir, réussir and about three hundred friends.

blocks.text: True second-group -ir verbs insert -iss- in all three plural forms. If a verb does that, it is regular; if it does not, it belongs with the irregulars in the third group.

Common members: finir, choisir, réussir, remplir, grandir, réfléchir, obéir, punir, applaudir, atterrir, ralentir. Many describe becoming something, and many are built from adjectives: grand → grandir, rouge → rougir.
Partir, sortir, dormir, servir and sentir look identical in the infinitive but have no -iss-. They drop their final stem consonant instead: je pars, je dors, je sors. They belong to the third group.

practice.why: Second-group plural takes -issons.
partir is third group: no -iss-, and the t of the stem drops.

practice.q: Which verb is a regular -ir verb?
practice.why: réussir takes -iss- in the plural; the other three do not.
ils → -issent.

title: Les verbes en -re au présent
summary: The smallest regular family, and the only one where the third person has no ending at all.

blocks.text: Members: attendre, vendre, entendre, répondre, perdre, descendre, rendre, défendre. The bare stem in the third person singular looks wrong to English eyes but is correct: il attend, il vend, il répond.

items.fr: J'attends le bus depuis vingt minutes.
items.en: I have been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes.
items.note: attendre needs no preposition — the 'for' is built in

items.fr: Elle répond à toutes les questions.
items.en: She answers all the questions.
items.note: répondre always takes à

blocks.text: Prendre looks like an -re verb and starts out like one, but goes irregular in the plural: nous prenons, ils prennent — the d disappears.

practice.why: Third person singular of an -re verb takes no ending.
nous → -ons.

practice.q: Which verb does NOT follow the regular -re pattern?
practice.why: prendre loses its d in the plural: nous prenons, ils prennent.
tu → -s.

title: Aller et le futur proche
summary: One irregular verb buys you the entire future tense.

blocks.text: Aller + infinitive is the everyday future in spoken French, exactly like English 'going to'. You can say almost anything about the future with it, and A1 learners do not need the futur simple at all.
To make it negative, wrap ne … pas around aller only, never around the infinitive: Je ne vais pas travailler demain.

items.fr: Ce week-end, je vais visiter le musée.
items.en: This weekend I'm going to visit the museum.

items.fr: Il ne va pas pleuvoir aujourd'hui.
items.en: It's not going to rain today.
items.note: ne … pas hugs va, not pleuvoir

items.fr: Nous allons à Montréal en train.
items.en: We're going to Montreal by train.
items.note: here aller is a real movement verb, not a future marker

blocks.text: Aller is also the verb for asking how someone is: comment allez-vous ? Literally 'how do you go?'

practice.why: nous → allons + infinitive.

practice.q: 'I'm not going to work tomorrow' is:
options: Je vais ne pas travailler demain.
Je ne vais pas travailler demain.
Je ne vais travailler pas demain.
practice.why: ne … pas surrounds the conjugated verb aller.
ils → vont.

practice.q: In 'je vais manger', what form is manger?
practice.why: After aller the second verb stays in the infinitive.

title: Le verbe faire
summary: To do, to make, and — surprisingly — the weather and every sport you play.

blocks.text: Vous faites and ils font are both irregular and both very common. Only three French verbs end in -tes for vous: être (vous êtes), dire (vous dites) and faire (vous faites).

head: Expression
Meaning
rows: faire du vélo / de la natation

blocks.text: Weather uses il fait + adjective, but rain and snow are their own verbs: il pleut, il neige. Never 'il fait pluie'.

practice.why: vous → faites, one of only three -tes forms in French.
Rain has its own verb, pleuvoir.
elles → font.
Weather takes the impersonal il fait.

title: La négation : ne … pas
summary: Two words that wrap around the verb — and one of them disappears when people speak.

blocks.text: French negation is a sandwich: ne goes before the conjugated verb, pas goes after it. Ne becomes n' before a vowel or silent h.
With a two-verb structure — aller + infinitive, or the passé composé — the sandwich closes around the first verb only. Je ne vais pas partir. Je n'ai pas compris.
In casual speech, ne is dropped almost entirely: je sais pas, c'est pas grave, j'ai pas faim. You should recognise this instantly, but write the full form in any exam.
Remember the article change: un, une, des and du all become de after a negation. Je n'ai pas de temps, not 'pas du temps'.

practice.q: Make negative: Il a des amis ici. → Il ___ ___ ___ ___ amis ici.
practice.why: n' before the vowel, pas after the verb, and des → d' before a vowel.
ne … pas surrounds the conjugated verb, not the infinitive.
Standard sandwich around comprend.
Dropping ne is normal in speech but not in writing.

title: Les questions fermées
summary: The same question in three levels of formality — pick one and be consistent.

head: Register
How to build it
Example
rows: keep the statement, raise your voice
invert verb and subject with a hyphen

blocks.text: All three mean exactly the same thing. Intonation dominates conversation, est-ce que is safe everywhere, and inversion belongs in writing, exams and polite service encounters.

Inversion has two mechanical rules. If the verb ends in a vowel and the subject is il, elle or on, insert -t- to make it pronounceable: a-t-il, va-t-elle, parle-t-on. If the subject is a noun, name it first and then invert with a pronoun: Marie est-elle là ?

items.fr: Est-ce que vous avez une table pour deux ?
items.en: Do you have a table for two?

items.fr: Parle-t-il anglais ?
items.en: Does he speak English?
items.note: -t- inserted between two vowels

items.fr: Ton frère travaille-t-il ici ?
items.en: Does your brother work here?
items.note: noun subject stated first, then inverted pronoun

blocks.text: To answer 'yes' to a negative question, French uses si instead of oui: — Tu n'aimes pas le café ? — Si, j'adore ça !

practice.why: Inversion is the formal register.

practice.q: Add the missing letter: A-___-il compris ?
practice.why: -t- is inserted between the vowel of a and il.

practice.q: — Tu n'as pas faim ? You ARE hungry. You answer:
practice.why: si contradicts a negative question.

practice.q: Make it neutral: Vous venez ce soir ? → ___ vous venez ce soir ?
practice.why: est-ce que placed in front converts any statement into a question.

title: Les mots interrogatifs
summary: Who, what, where, when, why, how much — and where they go in the sentence.

blocks.text: Quel is an adjective, so it agrees with the noun it asks about: quel jour, quelle heure, quels livres, quelles questions. All four forms sound identical.
In everyday speech the question word often slides to the end of the sentence: Tu habites où ? Tu pars quand ? C'est combien ? This is perfectly normal French and worth being able to hear.

items.fr: Quelle heure est-il ?
items.en: What time is it?
items.note: heure is feminine → quelle

items.fr: Pourquoi est-ce que tu apprends le français ?
items.en: Why are you learning French?

items.fr: Combien de temps ça prend ?
items.en: How long does it take?
items.note: combien de + noun

blocks.text: Answering pourquoi requires parce que, not car in speech: — Pourquoi ? — Parce que j'aime les langues.

practice.q: ___ est votre nom, s'il vous plaît ?
practice.why: nom is masculine singular.
heure is feminine singular.

practice.q: 'How many brothers do you have?' is:
practice.why: combien is always followed by de before a noun.

practice.q: — Pourquoi tu es en retard ? — ___ le bus était en retard.
practice.why: parce que introduces the reason.

title: L'accord des adjectifs
summary: Adjectives copy the gender and number of their noun. Four possible forms, often one sound.

blocks.text: The default rule: add -e for feminine, -s for plural, -es for both. If the adjective already ends in -e, the feminine adds nothing: rouge, rouge. If it already ends in -s or -x, the masculine plural adds nothing: français, français.

head: Masculine ending
Feminine
Example
rows: naturel → naturelle, italien → italienne, bon → bonne

blocks.text: Five very common adjectives are fully irregular and have a third masculine form used before a vowel.

items.fr: un bel appartement
items.en: a beautiful flat
items.note: bel because appartement starts with a vowel

items.fr: une vieille maison blanche
items.en: an old white house
items.note: both adjectives take the feminine

items.fr: des étudiants sérieux et travailleurs
items.en: serious, hard-working students

blocks.text: Colour adjectives derived from nouns never change: des yeux marron, une veste orange. Compound colours freeze too: des chaussures bleu foncé.

practice.why: -eux becomes -euse in the feminine.
hôtel starts with a silent h, so beau becomes bel.

options: marron comes from a noun (chestnut) and never agrees
practice.why: Colours named after objects are invariable.
-en doubles the n and adds -es.

title: La place des adjectifs
summary: Most follow the noun. A short list goes in front — and a few change meaning depending on which side they sit.

blocks.text: The French default is the opposite of English: the adjective comes after the noun. une voiture rouge, un livre intéressant, un homme sympathique.
A small set goes before the noun. The usual memory hook is BAGS: Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size.
Some adjectives sit on either side and change meaning as they move. This is not stylistic — it is a different word.

head: Adjective
Before the noun
After the noun
rows: un ancien collègue — a former colleague
un bâtiment ancien — an old building
un cher ami — a dear friend
un livre cher — an expensive book
un grand homme — a great man
un homme grand — a tall man
ma propre voiture — my own car
une voiture propre — a clean car
la dernière semaine — the final week

blocks.text: When a BAGS adjective sits before a plural noun, des often softens to de in careful writing: de bons amis rather than des bons amis. You will hear both.

practice.why: Colours always follow the noun.
Before the noun, ancien means former.
grand is a BAGS size adjective, so it precedes.

practice.q: 'un homme grand' describes someone who is:
practice.why: After the noun, grand is literal height.

title: Les adjectifs possessifs
summary: My, your, his, her — and the fact that French does not care whose it is, only what it is.

blocks.text: The crucial difference from English: the form agrees with the thing owned, not the owner. Son livre is 'his book' or 'her book' — French does not tell you which, and context has to. Sa voiture is 'his car' or 'her car'.
Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel, ma, ta and sa switch to mon, ton, son for pronunciation: mon amie, ton école, son adresse. The noun is still feminine — only the sound has changed.

items.fr: Marie parle à son père et à sa mère.
items.en: Marie is talking to her father and her mother.
items.note: son with père (m), sa with mère (f) — both mean 'her'

items.fr: Mon amie s'appelle Sophie.
items.en: My friend is called Sophie.
items.note: mon before a feminine noun starting with a vowel

items.fr: Nos collègues arrivent à neuf heures.
items.en: Our colleagues arrive at nine.

blocks.text: With body parts, French usually replaces the possessive with the definite article: je me lave les mains, il a mal à la tête. Saying 'je lave mes mains' sounds oddly clinical.

practice.why: sœur is feminine, so sa — even though the owner is male.
amie is feminine but starts with a vowel, so ma becomes mon.
The possessive agrees with livre, not with the owner.
Plural thing owned → leurs.

title: Les adjectifs démonstratifs
summary: One word for both 'this' and 'that' — French only distinguishes them when it needs to.

head: Form
Used before
Example
rows: masculine singular before a vowel or silent h

blocks.text: Ce livre covers both 'this book' and 'that book'. When the difference genuinely matters, French adds -ci (here) or -là (there) to the noun with a hyphen.

items.fr: Je préfère cette veste-ci à cette veste-là.
items.en: I prefer this jacket to that one.

items.fr: Cet hôtel est complet ce soir.
items.en: This hotel is full tonight.
items.note: cet because hôtel begins with a silent h

items.fr: Ces exercices sont difficiles.
items.en: These exercises are difficult.

blocks.text: In practice -là does most of the work in speech, even when it means 'this': ce truc-là. -ci sounds slightly bookish on its own.

practice.why: homme starts with a silent h, so ce becomes cet.
voiture is feminine singular.

practice.q: How do you contrast 'this one' with 'that one'?
practice.why: -ci marks near, -là marks far.
Plural takes ces.

title: Les nombres
summary: Regular up to sixty-nine, then arithmetic. Blame the Celts.

blocks.text: The number 1 uses et without a hyphen in 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71: vingt et un, soixante et onze. From 81 onwards the et disappears: quatre-vingt-un.
Quatre-vingts takes an -s when it stands alone, and loses it when another number follows: quatre-vingts euros, but quatre-vingt-deux euros. The same applies to cent: deux cents, but deux cent cinq.

items.fr: Ça coûte quatre-vingt-quinze dollars.
items.en: That costs ninety-five dollars.

items.fr: Il y a soixante-dix-huit pages.
items.en: There are seventy-eight pages.

items.fr: Mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-quinze.
items.en: Nineteen ninety-five.
items.note: years are read out in full, not in pairs

blocks.text: In Belgium and Switzerland you will hear septante (70) and nonante (90), which are far easier. They are not accepted in French exams, but they exist.

practice.why: 60 + 11, with et before onze.
4×20 + 12, no -s because a number follows.
quatre-vingts keeps its -s when nothing follows it.
et joins the unit 1 to the tens, with no hyphens.

title: L'heure
summary: Two systems: the conversational one with quarters, and the twenty-four hour clock used everywhere official.

blocks.text: The question is Quelle heure est-il ? and the answer always starts with Il est.

head: Time
Conversational
Official (24h)
rows: Il est deux heures et quart.
Il est trois heures et demie.
Il est cinq heures moins le quart.
Il est six heures moins dix.

blocks.text: After the half hour, French counts backwards from the next hour using moins. 4:45 is 'five o'clock minus the quarter'. This trips people up constantly, so practise it out loud.
To place an event in a part of the day, add du matin, de l'après-midi or du soir: à huit heures du soir. Timetables, appointments and TV listings all use the 24-hour clock instead.
Demie agrees after heure (feminine): trois heures et demie. But after midi and minuit (masculine) it does not: midi et demi.

practice.q: 10:45 conversationally: Il est ___ heures moins le quart.
practice.why: Count back from the next hour: eleven minus a quarter.
demie agrees with the feminine heures.
The 24-hour clock does not use et demie.
midi is masculine, so demi takes no -e.

title: La date et les jours
summary: Lowercase, cardinal numbers, and the one exception on the first of the month.

blocks.text: Days and months are never capitalised in French: lundi, janvier. The pattern for a date is le + number + month: le 14 juillet, le 3 mai 2026.
Use ordinary counting numbers for every day of the month except the first, which uses premier: le premier janvier, then le deux janvier, le trois janvier.

head: Question
Answer
rows: Je suis né le premier mai.

blocks.text: With days, the article changes the meaning. Lundi means 'on Monday' (this coming one). Le lundi means 'on Mondays' (every week).

items.fr: Lundi, j'ai un entretien.
items.en: On Monday I have an interview.
items.note: one specific Monday

items.fr: Le lundi, je travaille de chez moi.
items.en: On Mondays I work from home.
items.note: a weekly habit

items.fr: En janvier, il fait très froid ; au printemps, ça va mieux.
items.en: In January it's very cold; in spring it's better.
items.note: en + month, but au printemps

blocks.text: Seasons split their prepositions: au printemps, but en été, en automne, en hiver. Spring is the odd one out.

practice.why: Only the first of the month uses the ordinal.

practice.q: 'Le samedi, je fais du sport' means:
practice.why: The article makes it habitual.
en été, en automne, en hiver — but au printemps.
Months are lowercase in French.

title: Il y a
summary: One frozen expression that never changes form, whatever follows it.

blocks.text: Il y a covers both 'there is' and 'there are'. It never becomes plural: il y a un livre, il y a trois livres. Learn it as a single unit.

head: Form
Use
Example
rows: Il y a une pharmacie ici.
Il n'y a pas de place.
y a-t-il … ? / est-ce qu'il y a … ?
Y a-t-il un train à midi ?
Il y avait beaucoup de monde.
Il y aura une réunion demain.

blocks.text: Il y a has a second, unrelated meaning: 'ago'. Placed before a period of time, it looks back from now. J'ai commencé il y a deux ans — I started two years ago.

items.fr: Il y a trois personnes dans la salle.
items.en: There are three people in the room.

items.fr: Il n'y a pas de problème.
items.en: There's no problem.
items.note: un/une/des → de after the negation

items.fr: Je suis arrivé au Canada il y a quatre ans.
items.en: I arrived in Canada four years ago.

blocks.text: Do not confuse il y a (there is) with c'est (it is). Il y a introduces existence; c'est identifies something already present: Il y a un livre sur la table. C'est le livre de Marie.

practice.why: Invariable, even with a plural noun.

practice.q: Negative: Il y a du pain. → Il ___ y a pas ___ pain.
practice.why: n' before y, and du becomes de.

practice.q: 'J'ai déménagé il y a un an' means:
practice.why: il y a + duration looks backwards.

practice.q: Which introduces something new into the scene?
practice.why: il y a states that something exists; c'est identifies it.

title: Les prépositions de lieu
summary: Where things are — and which prepositions demand de afterwards.

head: Preposition
Meaning
Example
rows: Les clés sont dans le sac.
Le livre est sur la table.
Le chat est sous la chaise.
Le jardin est derrière la maison.
La poste est entre la banque et le café.
Le cinéma est à côté du parc.
L'école est en face de l'église.

blocks.text: The compound prepositions all end in de, which then contracts with the article: de + le = du, de + les = des. À côté du parc, en face des magasins, près de la gare.
Chez is uniquely French: it means at or to a person's home or business. Chez moi, chez le dentiste, chez Renault. It is always followed by a person, never a place name.
dans le bus but en voiture, en train, en avion, à pied, à vélo. Transport prepositions do not follow the logic of place prepositions — memorise them as a set.

practice.q: La pharmacie est à côté ___ supermarché.
practice.why: de + le contracts to du.
chez is used for going to a professional.

practice.q: 'The keys are on the table' is:
options: Les clés sont dans la table.
Les clés sont sur la table.
practice.why: sur means on top of.
de + les contracts to des.

title: À et de + l'article
summary: Four contractions that are compulsory, not optional.

blocks.text: There is no choice here. Writing 'je vais à le cinéma' is not a stylistic slip, it is ungrammatical. The contraction is as automatic as English 'don't' being possible but 'do not' also existing — except French has no uncontracted option.
De also expresses possession, where English uses an apostrophe: la voiture de Marie is Marie's car. French has no possessive apostrophe at all.

items.fr: Je vais au travail en voiture.
items.en: I go to work by car.

items.fr: C'est le livre du professeur.
items.en: It's the teacher's book.

items.fr: Elle joue aux cartes avec ses amis.
items.en: She plays cards with her friends.
items.note: jouer à + les cartes

blocks.text: Two verb families depend on this: jouer à for sports and games (jouer au foot), jouer de for instruments (jouer du piano).

practice.why: à + le always contracts to au.
de + les contracts to des.
Instruments take jouer de.

practice.q: Il revient ___ (de + le) bureau à six heures.
practice.why: de + le contracts to du.

title: Pouvoir, vouloir, devoir
summary: Three irregular verbs that carry an infinitive behind them and do all the work of politeness.

blocks.text: All three are followed directly by an infinitive with no preposition: je peux venir, je veux partir, je dois travailler.

The conditional forms of these verbs are the politeness system of French. Je veux un café is what a child says; je voudrais un café is what an adult says. Learn the polite forms now, before you need them.

items.fr: Je voudrais réserver une table pour deux.
items.en: I'd like to book a table for two.

items.fr: Pourriez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
items.en: Could you repeat, please?

items.fr: Il faut partir maintenant.
items.en: We have to leave now.
items.note: il faut is the impersonal alternative to devoir

blocks.text: Devoir also means 'to owe': je te dois vingt euros. Context separates the two meanings cleanly.

practice.why: nous → devons.

practice.q: Politest way to order a coffee:
practice.why: The conditional voudrais is the standard polite request.
vous → pouvez.

practice.q: After pouvoir, the next verb is in the:
practice.why: All three modal verbs take a bare infinitive.

title: Les verbes pronominaux
summary: Verbs that carry an extra pronoun because the subject acts on itself.

blocks.text: A reflexive verb has a pronoun between the subject and the verb, matching the subject. The infinitive is listed with se: se lever, se laver, s'appeler.
Many reflexive verbs also exist without the pronoun, and the difference is who receives the action. Je lave la voiture — I wash the car. Je me lave — I wash myself.

head: Verb
Meaning
rows: to get up / to go to bed

blocks.text: In the passé composé every reflexive verb takes être, without exception: je me suis levé, elle s'est habillée. There are no reflexive verbs that use avoir.

practice.why: je takes the pronoun me.
vous appears twice: once as the pronoun, once as the subject.

practice.q: In the passé composé, reflexive verbs take:
practice.why: Always être.
The nous form repeats nous.

title: Le passé composé avec avoir
summary: The main past tense of spoken French: avoir in the present, plus a past participle.

blocks.text: The passé composé describes a completed action in the past. It is built from two pieces: the auxiliary avoir conjugated in the present, and the past participle of the main verb.
Negation wraps around the auxiliary only, and adverbs like déjà, bien, souvent slide between the auxiliary and the participle: je n'ai pas mangé, j'ai déjà mangé, j'ai bien dormi.

items.fr: Hier, j'ai travaillé jusqu'à vingt heures.
items.en: Yesterday I worked until eight p.m.

items.fr: Nous n'avons pas compris la question.
items.en: We didn't understand the question.

items.fr: Elle a déjà envoyé le courriel.
items.en: She has already sent the email.

blocks.text: The participle after avoir does not agree with the subject: elle a mangé, never 'elle a mangée'. Agreement only happens with être, or when a direct object comes before the verb — a rule you meet at A2.

practice.why: avoir in the present plus the -é participle.

practice.q: Ils ___ ___ (prendre) le train de huit heures.
practice.why: prendre has the irregular participle pris.
ne … pas surrounds the auxiliary.
faire → fait, and no agreement after avoir.

title: Le passé composé avec être
summary: Fourteen movement verbs plus every reflexive verb — and here the participle does agree.

blocks.text: A small group of verbs, almost all about movement or change of state, builds the passé composé with être instead of avoir. With être, the past participle behaves like an adjective and agrees with the subject.

Every reflexive verb also uses être: je me suis levé(e), nous nous sommes couché(e)s. And six of the movement verbs switch to avoir when they take a direct object: j'ai monté les valises (I took the suitcases up) versus je suis monté (I went up).

items.fr: Elle est arrivée à Montréal en 2022.
items.en: She arrived in Montreal in 2022.
items.note: feminine subject → arrivée

items.fr: Nous sommes sortis très tard hier soir.
items.en: We went out very late last night.

items.fr: Je me suis couché à minuit.
items.en: I went to bed at midnight.
items.note: reflexive → être

blocks.text: The traditional memory aid is the house of être — imagine a house you enter, climb, stay in, fall down in, and leave. Every verb in the story takes être.

practice.why: aller takes être, and the feminine subject adds -e.
venir takes être, masculine plural adds -s.
partir takes être and agrees with the feminine subject.

practice.q: 'J'ai monté les valises' uses avoir because:
practice.why: With a direct object, monter switches to avoir.

title: L'impératif
summary: Giving instructions: drop the pronoun, and drop one letter from -er verbs.

blocks.text: The imperative exists in only three persons: tu, nous and vous. You form it by taking the present tense and removing the subject pronoun.
For -er verbs, the tu form loses its final -s: tu parles becomes parle. The same applies to aller (va) and to -ir verbs conjugated like -er verbs (ouvre, offre).
Four verbs are irregular: être (sois, soyons, soyez), avoir (aie, ayons, ayez), savoir (sache, sachons, sachez) and vouloir (veuillez, used only for very polite requests).
With reflexive verbs, the pronoun moves after the verb and te becomes toi: lève-toi, dépêchez-vous. In the negative it moves back in front: ne te lève pas.

items.fr: Écoutez bien et répétez après moi.
items.en: Listen carefully and repeat after me.

items.fr: Ne t'inquiète pas, tout va bien.
items.en: Don't worry, everything is fine.
items.note: negative reflexive: pronoun goes back before the verb

items.fr: Veuillez patienter quelques instants.
items.en: Please wait a few moments.
items.note: the most formal imperative in French

blocks.text: The -s comes back before y and en for pronunciation: vas-y ! (go on!), manges-en ! (have some!).

practice.why: -er verbs drop the final -s in the tu imperative.
Affirmative reflexive imperative puts the pronoun after with a hyphen.

practice.q: The imperative of être for vous is:
practice.why: être is irregular: sois, soyons, soyez.
In the negative the reflexive pronoun returns before the verb.

title: C'est ou il est ?
summary: Two ways to say 'it is' that are not interchangeable — decide by what comes next.

blocks.text: The rule is mechanical: look at the word immediately after. If it is a noun with a determiner (un, le, mon…), use c'est. If it is a bare adjective or an unmodified profession, use il/elle est.

head: Use
When followed by
Example
rows: an adjective about a specific thing

blocks.text: The profession pair is the one worth drilling: Il est médecin and C'est un médecin both mean 'he is a doctor'. The moment an article appears, you must switch to c'est.

items.fr: — Qui est-ce ? — C'est mon frère. Il est développeur.
items.en: — Who is it? — That's my brother. He's a developer.

items.fr: Ce livre ? Il est très intéressant.
items.en: This book? It's very interesting.
items.note: adjective about a specific book

items.fr: Apprendre une langue, c'est difficile.
items.en: Learning a language is difficult.
items.note: general comment → c'est, always masculine singular

blocks.text: General statements are always c'est + masculine singular adjective, whatever the subject: la grammaire, c'est compliqué — not 'compliquée'.

practice.why: Followed by an article + noun.
Profession with no article → elle est.
Once un appears, you need c'est.
Plural noun takes ce sont.
